Recent findings suggest that on one occasion, my server was a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon, as painters have done for decades. He met Ross Bleckner there, and David Salle. He used to have a massive loft studio in Williamsburg, but as rents went up, he moved deeper into Brooklyn, to Fort Greene, where he built a studio in his basement.

Recent findings suggest that the twist is that my server’s art was also hanging on the walls of Borgo, as was his daughter’s art. That’s because he was Andrew Tarlow—the painter and restaurateur who kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic with his restaurant Diner and, yes, also owns Borgo.

It has been revealed that after launching that instant hit in an old, reclaimed diner, Tarlow opened five more era-defining Brooklyn spots before finally venturing into Manhattan with Borgo. All along, he’s still been the artist who got a job at The Odeon so that he could meet his heroes. He’s still painting away in his brownstone, doodling on notepads during concept meetings. He’s had demonstrates recently at galleries such as Tiwa Select; he’s loosely associated with the Galerie Sardine extended universe; and he’s someone whose work I’ve been told about for years by those in the know.

As they put it, Tarlow is an emerging artist who happens to own the best all-around restaurant in Manhattan, as well as a bunch of other successful spots in Brooklyn.

“I realized, opening Borgo, that I really loved working in restaurants—and not that I had forgotten, but I hadn’t actually worked services in a while until I opened,” Tarlow told me during a studio visit. “And then, in a similar way, I think—I love making paintings. I actually will paint forever, no matter what happens.”.

The studio had dozens of unstretched canvases heaped on the ground, some still rolled up, and others hanging via a pin on the studio wall. They highlighted figures grappling with pain in fierce color-blocked fields, automatic-painting abstractions, faces fading into other faces. One painting was a portrait of the artist Joe Bradley, a friend.

In a recent development, the studio is in the basement of the Fort Greene brownstone where Tarlow has lived for two decades with his wife, Kate Huling, raising four kids in a kind of neo-boho paradise. There were no studio assistants, no art handlers, no frames, no boxes, no packaging—just the artist and the work.

“It was kind of just as chaotic as everything else there, but in the most perfect warm embrace of a way. I saw the pure energy that he put into his paintings and the stories that they told,” says Alex Tieghi-Walker, the founder of Tiwa Select, calling from London. “So many artists could be quite—rightfully so, but quite precious with their works. And I love that Andrew was just like, ‘Oh, pull out the ones you’re taking and just take them in an Uber home.’”.

Tarlow grabbed at a canvas bare-handed, one with a bit of a conceptual bent, and put it up on an easel.

“I’ve had this up on the wall for a while now, and I just continued to look at it because I’m happy with it. I’m also a little unsettled—I mean, I’m showing you the inside of my drawers. I’m also a little unsettled by how far it’s gone abstract-wise.”.

He told me he couldn’t really do his other job, the restaurant job, without painting at odd hours. They’re totally separate, but complementary in a cosmic way.

“What are the processes? Like you stated, for some people, it’s nine to five. Then you listen to the news, smoke a cigarette, drink coffee. It’s either working or it’s not. The door either opens or it’s not,” Tarlow said, gesturing around to his studio. “But I’m going to go here every day, and I’m going to push some paint on canvas.”.

According to recent reports, diner opened in 1999, a few years after Tarlow moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg—where the crumbling street dead-ends into the East River. While looking for a cheap studio space, he found a 6,000-square-foot loft across the street from an abandoned diner from the 1920s. The loft’s landlord bought the diner, and in 1999, Tarlow opened Diner with then partner Mark Firth—and watched as it was patronized by only the artists across the street.

“You could stand outside the restaurant in those days and not see a single person walk by,” he told Bon Appetit in 2010.

According to recent reports, tarlow kept expanding. He opened Marlow & Sons, and then the butcher shop and specialty food store Marlow & Daughters. He founded a bakery, She Wolf, and a literary magazine, Diner Journal. He operated the restaurant at the Wythe Hotel, but only for a few years. Instead of doing the easy thing, Vegas-ifying Diner in some newly introduced development on the Williamsburg waterfront, he got even weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far-out corner of Greenpoint.

Industry observers note that A dealer with a gallery in Tribeca was the first, but far from the last, to tell me I had to check out Tarlow’s paintings. After an introduction was brokered, Tarlow invited me to lunch at Borgo this past summer. The restaurant has many fantastic pork-laden dishes, but we ate almost entirely vegetables, as well as one very elegant, simple piece of fish. A summer lunch. We fell into an easy patter, talking about exhibitions, other artists—but mostly his painting practice. He’d been working on Long Island, not on the East End but in the middle. He’d had a few demonstrates. There was discussion of representation. He spoke about all this with an unpracticed earnestness and complete confidence. He sounded like a very prominent emerging artist, which, at 56, he is.

It has been revealed that “I don’t know if it’s just age or time, or I was too much of a young person, or a young mind, but I’ve been more secure with my ability to hold all these things in the same time,” he told me back in the studio. “I can go work tonight in the restaurant and feel perfectly confident in that work, and I can show you this work and feel perfectly confident in this work. Whereas, I think, as a young person, I felt like, Am I fake?”.

Sometimes it’s not the enfant terrible who breaks out—it’s the working parent, the person with a desk job, the successful entrepreneur who back-ends into revolutionary art making. Think William Carlos Williams writing “The Red Wheelbarrow” while working as a doctor in Rutherford, Upcoming Jersey. Or Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children in San Francisco. Or Jeff Koons working on Wall Street in order to earn money to make his sculptures. Having a demanding job actually granted them the freedom to be artists. Tarlow started drawing during restaurant concept meetings.

Sometimes Tarlow hangs his own paintings upstairs in his brownstone’s salon room, or at his house on Long Island, to see what they look like in the wild. The paintings have a confident thrust to them, with the colors bold-blocked in a way that reminds me of Albert Oehlen, drawing from Roman and Greek mythology in Twombly-esque riffs: visages multiplying and fading like a Kippenberger-ian pomo ride into the ether. Sure, any painter who’s spent time in Europe since the 1990s has wanted to be Martin Kippenberger. But Tarlow has an actual connection to him: Like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a lover of Italian food and good wine, and he made art to hang in restaurants. And like Tarlow, Kippenberger was a restaurant owner, balancing his studio practice with running Capri, a Venice, California, spot in which he invested after moving to Los Angeles in 1989. According to those present at the time, Kippenberger became a part-owner of the place because, as the artist put it, “You can’t get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles.”.

As a bartender at The Odeon, Tarlow maintained a working painting studio but found it hard to produce art. After opening Diner, he skipped painting sessions in favor of opening businesses and starting a family. Once that duality settled, he started drawing on the move, carrying sketchbooks and working through potential paintings. Eventually, once the kids got old enough, he built out a studio in a nook of his 19th-century basement.

“I really started painting back downstairs. Let’s just say, after dinner, it was 8 p.m. and they were watching Nemo. No one actually needs me, they’re totally happy. My wife’s up there, everyone’s laughing, giggling with little fish,” he mentioned. “And I can just walk down here and do my thing. Having it in my house for sure is the only way I could do this amount of work, and for sure even get to this place. Because I do think you have to do a certain amount of work to get to this place unless you’re just a born prodigy. But when you think about the genius of Picasso or whomever, he made a million fucking paintings.”.

Tarlow didn’t really show anyone his work for a long time.

“I met Andrew socially. I knew his restaurants way before I knew Andrew. And one day he was like, ‘Come and see my studio,’” Tieghi-Walker tells me. “It did not surprise me at all that he had an art studio in his basement and that these were the types of works he was creating.”.

Recent findings suggest that the show at Tiwa Select was on view right as Tarlow was getting ready to open Borgo. There was a certain amount of unconscious transference, Tarlow told me. For the Tiwa dinner, instead of creating name placards, the artist hand-sketched an artwork of each guest’s name on the paper tablecloth. Now, when a regular makes a reservation at Borgo, Tarlow will elegantly sketch out their name on the paper tablecloth.

Recent findings suggest that the showcasing of his art at Borgo marks the first time Tarlow has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant. Tarlow doesn’t exactly promote this. When I asked about it, he told me that only one of his own works was up at the moment, then changed the subject. Alex Levy, the media strategist and theater producer, has been a regular at Borgo since it opened. “Borgo is the grown-up Platonic ideal of what a restaurant can be,” he said. After several visits, Levy, who also collects a bit of contemporary art, noticed what was on the walls.

“I complimented one of the paintings, and Andrew mentioned, ‘It’s by my daughter.’ And then he pointed to another one and said, ‘That’s by me,’” Levy claims. “I had no idea that there’s this whole other part of him.”.

According to recent reports, like Tarlow, Levy balances two seemingly divergent but strangely complementary careers—as a speechwriter on one hand, a Tony Award winner on the other—and Tarlow invited him to see his studio on Long Island. Levy bought a painting immediately. Seeing the studio, Levy says, helped him realize, to some extent, what the special sauce is behind a place like Borgo. It’s for incredibly confident, hyperproductive creative types, run by an artist who has complete faith in his ability to work.

And for Tarlow, the focus and passion in one arena lead right into the passion for the other.

“I’m also being very present for your needs in the same way as I’m trying to be very present with these paintings,” he mentioned. “They’re not separate boats. When the restaurant’s working, I feel creative inside of it.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Wisconsin woman will spend the next several years in prison after she admitted to abusing a patient with disabilities by repeatedly hitting him with his favorite toy.

Toyo Perez pleaded guilty to four counts of patient abuse and five counts of abusing an individual at risk in August. Three months after Perez, 50, entered her plea, Rock County Circuit Judge Derrick Grubb sentenced her to serve 13 years in prison. Once she is no longer incarcerated, she will serve an additional nine years of extended supervision.

The investigation into Perez’s abuse began in January, when members of the Rock County Sheriff’s Office were shown a video that captured her hitting an adult patient with disabilities, according to WKOW’s courtroom report.

According to recent reports, after authorities became aware of the abuse, detectives discovered more than a dozen videos documenting similar acts of abuse. The Rock County District Attorney’s Office said that the footage showed Perez striking and pushing the man over and over, while she was also seen twisting the man’s ear and beating him with a hard plastic weighted baby doll — what prosecutors described as his “favorite” toy.

“She was there to care for him,” prosecutor Verity Altenberger told the judge in court. “There is no ‘why.’ This was not one bad day. This was multiple times per day, for multiple days, over weeks.”.

The prosecutor added that Perez’s abuse was “pure cruelty.”.

Meanwhile, Perez’s defense attorney argued that her treatment of the victim was a result of stress.

Law enforcement said that the victim is an adult male who has significant autism and developmental delays, with an approximate cognitive level similar to that of a 1-year-old child.

Family members remarked they initially believed the victim remained calm around Perez because they shared a special connection, but prosecutors said they later learned that his subdued state was a result of the abuse and an instilled sense of fear.

After Perez pleaded guilty, the state requested a sentence of 24 years in prison while the defense requested she simply serve probation time.

Once the judge determined Perez’s sentence, he spoke to her about the gravity of her crimes.

#154477. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1291 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Lifehacker ↗ Open Full Page

Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1291 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now.
  • According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt.
  • Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”.

According to recent reports, at this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

Industry observers note that to borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

According to recent reports, the problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Industry observers note that those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”.

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic.".

Sources indicate that if there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

Industry observers note that in every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

It has been revealed that this is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

Sources indicate that I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

Sources indicate that to a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

People online (via Gizmodo) are theorizing that the crashing challenges with GTA 6 on PS5 might be due to the game's intense demands on the hardware, and it could be specifically tied to older PS5s. https://twitter.com/ghost_motley/status/2123465979791380670?s=20 Rockstar has yet to officially respond to these reports. Rockstar's official GTA 6 error troubleshooting page isn't much help, as it only links to the support sites for PlayStation and Xbox and offers no specific help. Players can submit a support ticket to Rockstar to get more help with this issue or others. These issues do not appear to be very widespread, but if you're experiencing the CE-108255-1 error on PS5, that's no consolation to you. After years of waiting, GTA fans can finally play GTA 6, but some players are encountering a dreaded error code that makes the game crash or otherwise fail.

It has been revealed that consumers are reporting receiving the CE-108255-1 error code, which players might see when a game crashes mid-session or fails to load entirely. Crashing mid-game in GTA 6 would be particularly frustrating given how saves work.

Sony's official word is that players can try updating their game to fix the matter. If it's really that simple, that would be a welcome result. But people are saying that doesn't always work and are asking Rockstar to put out an official patch.

In a recent development, reddit user Acrobatic-Promise458 encountered this issue and documented their experience. The person noted the game was working normally until they reached a certain point in the story, at which point the game crashes continually. They said Rockstar support directed them to Sony's own support team, but it was no use.

People online (via Gizmodo) are theorizing that the crashing complications with GTA 6 on PS5 might be due to the game's intense demands on the hardware, and it could be specifically tied to older PS5s.

Rockstar has yet to officially respond to these reports. Rockstar's official GTA 6 error troubleshooting page isn't much help, as it only links to the support sites for PlayStation and Xbox and offers no specific help. Players can submit a support ticket to Rockstar to get more help with this concern or others.

These issues do not appear to be very widespread, but if you're experiencing the CE-108255-1 error on PS5, that's no consolation to you.

GTA 6 has reportedly sold 25 million copies and earned more than $2 billion in revenue already, and those numbers are only expected to grow higher.

This is the November 20, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Sources indicate that it’s True Colors, from New York, where over the course of a few days billions of dollars have been spent at auction houses. Nvidia has lost more than $2 trillion in market cap since early October, but on Thursday, Anthropic’s IPO minted a class of new billionaires. It’s whiplash. As one dazed art dealer mused aloud on Monday night in the elevator at Sotheby’s: “It seems like money’s lost all its value.” Maybe the money, but not the art. Amid a surreal era of wealth creation and artificial intelligence, once-in-a-century oil-on-canvas masterpieces only get more covetable. Two Van Goghs from the same collectors have now sold for $190 million apiece, both in the span of a year.

Recent findings suggest that one thing remains constant: Everybody has to eat dinner. And increasingly, they’re doing it at Borgo, perhaps the best all-around restaurant in New York—where the owner is a semisecret acclaimed painter. I talked to Andrew Tarlow about maintaining a practice as a serious, boundary-pushing painter while running a Manhattan restaurant.

It has been revealed that speaking of restaurateurs: Michael Chow opened his first Mr. Chow in London nearly 60 years ago, and the spot is still as good as ever. A few works from Chow’s collection, some made specifically for the restaurant, are on view at Gagosian on Madison Avenue. I recently spent some time with him (and, briefly, Larry Gagosian) going through works by Ed Ruscha, Julian Schnabel, Jean-Michel Basquiat, and Andy Warhol, as well as many portraits of Chow himself.

We’ve also got reports from the Baby2Baby Gala in LA, the Ballroom Marfa Gala in Harlem, and a special dinner in Tribeca. And all the gossip from the auctions.

Mentioned in this issue: William Acquavella, Steve Wynn, Steve Cohen, Patrick Drahi, Charles Stewart, Jackie Wachter, Anthony Haden-Guest, Leonardo DiCaprio, Vittoria Ceretti, Jeff Koons, Frances Outred, Andrew Tarlow, Walter Isaacson, Matthew Schneier, Ross Bleckner, David Salle, Valentina Akerman, Joe Bradley, Kate Huling, Alex Tieghi-Walker, Alex Levy, Albert Oehlen, Ignacio Mattos, Louis Shannon, Victoire Bourgois, Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin, Meredith Darrow, Annie Morris, Michael Chow, Lady Gaga, Jim Dine, and Larry Gagosian.

Van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, including fees, Wednesday night at Sotheby’s Breuer building headquarters on Madison. It’s the most expensive work sold at auction this year, and easily among the top 10 priciest things to ever be publicly auctioned. It’s a bit insane to say this, especially about a single canvas that sold for more than the total value of the art set to be on offer at Art Basel Miami Beach next month, but that price feels a bit like a…disappointment? The on-request estimate for the work was $180 million, and the hammer price fell well short of that, at $165 million. Bidding in the room was thin, and the lot was guaranteed by Sotheby’s. Though it’s unclear where the exact guarantee price landed, it was probably around the estimate.

Honestly, it’s a relief to the house and the seller—the family of the Argentinian collectors Carlos Pedro Blaquier and Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier—that this painting sold at all. A Jewish collector bought the work in 1909 from a Paris gallery. His heirs claimed, just days before the auction, that the work was later sold under duress due to Nazi persecution, entitling them to receive restitution. The parties came together over an eleventh hour deal, terms undisclosed, to allow the sale to go through.

Sources indicate that so who bought it? The winning bidder in the room was William Acquavella, the patriarch of one of Newly introduced York’s great art-dealing families, who has an august gallery on the Upper East Side. It’s unclear for whom he bought it. In the past he’s been known to broker art deals on behalf of former Las Vegas casino tycoon Steve Wynn. In 2013, Acquavella was the winning bidder on a Francis Bacon tryptic for $142 million—that time on behalf of Wynn’s ex-wife, the late Elaine Wynn. (The piece is currently on view at LACMA, where Elaine Wynn was a co-chair of the board.) Steve Wynn has been more of a seller than a buyer recently, so the jury’s still out on whom Acquavella was on the phone with Wednesday.

The $190 million price tag is an almost exact match for the amount someone else paid for another Van Gogh from the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Reports say that, in 2025, Christie’s conducted a private sale where Le Zouave, a Van Gogh portrait of a soldier, sold for $190 million. While there’s no indication that the most recent buyer was someone connected to the AI gold rush, it’s surely indicative of the times that a Van Gogh has sold for 9 figures right around the moment that the seven cofounders of Anthropic have become worth about $20 billion—and around 600 Anthropic employees have become worth more than $100 million. When reached for comment through a rep, Acquavella didn’t get back to me.

— As I walked into Sotheby’s Monday for the first sales of the week, there were clients going downstairs to get their tables at Marcel, where diners can bid tableside while cocktails are served from a bar cart. Other clients went to a sumptuous overflow room with an open bar and a large spread of Marcel goodies. Those lucky enough to snag seats moseyed up to the sales room, where telecom billionaire Patrick Drahi, the owner of Sotheby’s, was standing in the back, near CEO Charles Stewart.

The 6 p.m. start time meant some collectors were still trickling in when Jackie Wachter snagged a Gerhard Richter work for a hammer price of $5 million. In the back of the room, white-jacketed waiters wheeled around with flutes of Champagne for those standing in the back. The writer Anthony Haden-Guest, a longtime Vanity Fair scribe whose book True Colors gave this column its name, walked in and took a seat in the back. One woman started taking selfies. As the contemporary sale got underway, Leonardo DiCaprio and his girlfriend, Vittoria Ceretti, walked down from the skybox and watched as an Agnes Martin hammered at $9.2 million. DiCaprio, a very serious collector, didn’t appear to be bidding, but no matter; he was still there at Sotheby’s. Auction week had officially begun.

Sources indicate that — Over at Christie’s, the house sold a Georgia O’Keeffe that had been on view in an apartment in my neighborhood for more than 60 years. Suffice to say, there aren’t many expensive works of art that get discovered in apartments in the vicinity of Tompkins Square Park. I had to savor the lot’s beautifully poetic provenance, a phrasing that I don’t believe has ever been printed in an auction catalog previously: “Property from an East Village Private Collection.” It sold for $4.9 million.

— The week’s hottest lot? Maybe a sculpture of a dog by Jeff Koons, Bob-Tail, that was first on view at the artist’s still-controversial “Made in Heaven” show. Estimated to sell for an ambitious high estimate of $3.5 million, it hammered at $9 million, or $9.7 million with fees. Former auction chairman Frances Outred mentioned the sculpture was consigned by a college friend of his who bought it from Anthony d’Offay for a five-figure sum in 1995, “when the art market was in the doldrums and the Jeff Koons market was at its nadir.”.

Industry observers note that — For a dinner on Tuesday, Galerie Sardine installed a long table where every seat had a great view of one of the Joe Bradley paintings that had been installed in a space on 9 White Street. It wasn’t exactly a tough sell to get the works at the dinner—Bradley is married to Galerie Sardine founder Valentina Akerman. The always exquisite Ignacio Mattos whipped up some Estela-level pinchos ahead of serving an unctuously rich rice-and-chicken dish.

According to recent reports, — Ballroom Marfa held its annual gala Thursday at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, which, as honoree Anne-Cecilie Engell Speyer reminded attendees, is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world. For context: The cathedral would take up nearly four whole blocks of downtown Marfa, Texas. In addition to Speyer, the honorees included photojournalist Lynsey Addario and musician Lyle Lovett, who was introduced by VF contributing photographer Mark Seliger. The evening raised $1.5 million for Ballroom Marfa.

It has been revealed that — After the auction on Wednesday, the gallery Entrance, a space opened by dealer Louis Shannon on Ludlow Street nearly a decade ago, hosted an opening for the painter Victoire Bourgois. Lots of artists were there to support her—Nate Lowman, Julian Schnabel, Dustin Yellin—and the event was followed by a dinner at the ultimate Dimes Square redoubt. That’s right: Dimes itself. Can you believe Dimes has been open for—checks age—more than 13 years? And guess what? After all the Dimes Square discourse, the actual restaurant itself still slaps.

Recent findings suggest that — The annual Baby2Baby Gala went down in LA last weekend. I wasn’t able to make it out West, but luckily for Vanity Fair, Tallulah Willis was on the scene and wrote a fabulous party report that you can read here. I also want to note that the live auction of artworks, curated, as always, by Darrow Contemporary founder Meredith Darrow, included an Annie Morris sculpture that achieved $410,000.

Industry observers note that on a Friday in November, I walk into Gagosian on Madison Avenue for a meeting with Michael Chow, the artist, collector, filmmaker, designer, actor, and founder of the restaurant Mr. Chow. There’s a portrait of Chow by Jean-Michel Basquiat, a portrait by Julian Schnabel, a portrait by Andy Warhol. There’s a drawing of Chow by David Hockney, made soon after Mr. Chow opened in London in 1968.

Michael Chow: So I opened that restaurant. You’ve got Hockney, you’ve got fashion, you’ve got every single thing. It’s almost like a Dada movement on the First World War thing. This one is in London—all happening.

He starts talking about duopolys: Christie’s versus Sotheby’s, Coke versus Pepsi. There was an Italian restaurant in London’s Soho, so he opened a Chinese restaurant in Soho with Italian waiters. He has a theory about name-dropping.

Chow: I hate people who drop names, and Lady Gaga agrees with me.

True Colors: That’s a good one.

According to recent reports, why is name-dropping important? Because the minute I say “Napoleon,” you will go there immediately. So it saves a lot of time. Okay, so why am I saying that? Do you know who Robert Fraser is?

The art dealer from the ’60s. Groovy Bob.

I was looking forward to meeting him, blah, blah, blah. He was sitting there. Name-dropping. Sitting in front is Jim Dine. Name-dropping again. I say, “I would like to borrow some paintings.” I mentioned, “Just like”—do you know the Kronenhalle restaurant?

We walk over to the Hockney portrait of Michael Chow sitting in his restaurant.

Chow: The first person I went to is David. He drew one and I remarked, “Boy.” You know what he did? Tore it all up.

Sources indicate that simultaneously, I went to Peter Blake. I say, “Give me a painting that’s the antithesis of racism,” which he did. At that time he’s into the circus, he’s into all that shit. All right? So I asked him, “Why did you do that?” He did a portrait. So now Peter Blake is fucking crazy. He loves the circus, he loves wrestling and all that shit.

Industry observers note that larry Gagosian walks in and gives Chow a fist bump. Gagosian takes a long look at the Schnabel and then flips through a book of drawings made by artists for 57th Street’s Mr. Chow when it was the art world’s clubhouse. We walk up to the Basquiat.

Recent findings suggest that true Colors: To have it as this sort of landscape, you have the horizon line here, but it’s almost like a Western. It’s almost cinematic.

Chow: Name me three classic Westerns.

Shane. The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance. High Noon.

Industry observers note that I’m going to act out the first scene of each. Okay, High Noon.

He uses his hand to pull a finger gun on me, then gets distracted by the Ed Ruscha and the Warhol double portrait.

Chow: Andy noted, “Oh, what do you want?” I said, “Hold the color and add lots of diamonds.”.

Gagosian brings up Anselm Kiefer, and then Richard Serra.

Chow: If you look at the year 2000, Charlie Rose and Richard Serra, their conversation on the culture of China, and Richard Serra identifies very clearly what is fine art: poetry, music, sculpture, and painting.

Recent findings suggest that the works in the show are for sale. I ask Chow if he’s emotional about parting with them. He seems very calm.

Chow: I’m only a temporary steward of the works.

“Friends and Legends: The Collection of Michael Chow” is up at Gagosian’s 980 Madison space until December 22.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Recent findings suggest that would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

According to recent reports, in the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.).

It has been revealed that in the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

It has been revealed that here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart swiftly led to women posting the waist heart.

According to recent reports, okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?".

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood.".

Sources indicate that nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lindsey Vonn is getting back out there after her ACL surgery — except she’s on a scooter instead of skis.

“First trip out of the house… of course it was to do some Christmas shopping with Chance and I had to bring back my scooter 🛴 💨 ,” Vonn, 42, wrote via Instagram on Monday, November 23, alongside a video of herself riding through a Michaels craft store with her dog.

“Nothing like a little arts and crafts at Michaels 🎄,” she continued. “IYKYK.”.

Vonn underwent surgery on her ACL on November 11, marking the ninth procedure the Olympic alpine skier has had on her left leg after two major downhill crashes earlier this year.

In a recent development, “It took over 5 hours to remove all of the plates and screws from my leg and replace my ACL,” Vonn wrote via Instagram on November 12. “I am home from the hospital now and thankful to be on the final road to a full recovery.”.

Before the procedure, Vonn admitted that she was “nervous and anxious” but “excited to hopefully put this behind me.”.

“This will be my 9th surgery and I’m praying my last. There are still things that could change in surgery, so we will have to wait and see how it goes, but I will keep you posted on my progress when I am out of surgery and recovering,” she wrote. “I am in the best hands though and thankful for the help of my doctors, physical therapist, nurses and medical staff 🙏🏻. Thank you again for all of the support over these last 9 months. It has truly meant the world to me to receive so much love and encouragement. 🙏🏻❤️ As my Mother mentioned, ‘Today is another great day!’… I hope she’s right 🙏🏻🤞🏻.”.

Check our latest news in Google News.

Check our latest news in Apple News.

It has been revealed that vonn completely ruptured her ACL in a crash during the final race of the World Cup season in Crans-Montana, Switzerland, in January. Despite the injury, she competed in the Winter Olympics days later and suffered a compound fracture and a tibial plateau fracture in another crash during the women’s downhill final on February 8.

Recent findings suggest that “I still have another surgery, so I’m trying to get as strong as possible,” Vonn told TNT Sports at the US Open in August. “And once I get my ACL, then I’ll have another long road ahead of me. But for now, I feel great, and I’m very thankful for that.”.

Recent findings suggest that she continued, “I’m hoping that I can have the [ACL] surgery in November, but it’ll be in the winter sometime, and then it’ll be another nine months until I’m fully recovered from that, so I can’t really look beyond that. I don’t really know what the future holds, but like I stated, I’m just thankful for where I am right now.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some major numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • Industry observers note that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some substantial numbers that speak to the pent-up demand.
  • For starters, the internet service provider Comcast announced that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the manufacturer's history in terms of demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some major numbers that speak to the pent-up demand. GTA 6 sold more than 30 million copies and hit almost $4 billion on day one, but that's just the start of understanding the impact of the game's release. For starters, the internet service provider Comcast unveiled that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the manufacturer's history in terms of demand. Peak traffic was 31% higher than an average day and a full 9.6% higher that the previous biggest day ever for traffic to Comcast's network. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA GTA 6 also now holds five of the top 10 busiest days of Comcast's network of all time. Going further, Comcast stated around 24% of all internet traffic on Comcast's network was people downloading or playing GTA 6 on November 18 (no doubt thanks to the New Zealand trick). Additionally, traffic to Twitch on Comcast's network was up by almost 50% and "is still increasing," Comcast said. A spokesperson for Comcast further contextualized the traffic data, telling GameSpot that between when preloading began on November 10 and through November 18, PlayStation and Xbox traffic pushed enough data on the network for one million homes to stream The Odyssey in 4K repeatedly for two days straight. Comcast was among the internet service providers that offered free speed boosts to subscribers to help them download GTA 6 faster. Additionally, Mat Piscatella of Circana shared data that speaks to the enormity of GTA 6's launch on PlayStation and Xbox. For active accounts November 19 in the US, 61% of PS5 accounts "engaged with" GTA 6. On Xbox, 56% of Xbox players globally did. PS5 players averaged 513 minutes of play for GTA 6 on November 19, compared to 494 on Xbox. These daily active user and minutes played figures are "absolutely bonkers," Piscatella said. GTA 6 was No. 1 on November 19, pushing Fortnite down to No. 2 based on these engagement metrics, Circana said. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you’re eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hallmark churns out nearly a hundred new romance movies every year. The 2026 Countdown to Christmas lineup alone is slated for 34 original holiday-themed flicks. Part of the reason it’s easy for the cable channel-turned-streamer to make so many movies a year is that it has a list of dedicated actors who are eager to star in these films -- like Queen of Hallmark Lacey Chabert. And yet, somehow, they manage to keep the pairings fresh. So fresh that two of my favorite longtime Hallmark actors, Erin Cahill and Andrew Walker, just starred in their first movie together. I’m happy to report it was worth the wait!

In a recent development, yep, you read that right. After spending 20 years with the cable channel and being friends for 18 years, Cahill and Walker finally got to share the screen as romantic leads in Christmas in Blue Dog Valley. The holiday flick follows Goldie MacKenzie (Cahil), a former Hollywood on-set veterinarian, who decides to leave the glitz and glamour for a slower life as the in-house veterinarian in the small town of Blue Dog Valley.

Industry observers note that the residents of Blue Dog Valley aren’t too thrilled about an outsider taking over their beloved veterinary practice, and Goldie has to work overtime to win over the hearts of the town’s loyal pet owners. Desperate for an ally, Goldie turns to Cohen (Walker), the son of the former owner of the vet practice, for help. While they get off to a rough start, sparks start to fly as the two spend more time together, especially with Goldie taking over planning duties for the annual Christmas parade that will feature the four-legged and furry residents of the town this year.

It’s not just their characters who have love for each other, though. Both Cahill and Walker have a deep appreciation for each other and their decades-long friendship. In talking with Hallmark on set, both of these iconic stars shared how excited they were to be sharing the screen together for the first time. Take a look:.

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel).

It can be easy for the human actors to get upstaged by their animal co-stars, especially when there are so many different types of animals in a movie (cows, alpacas, and of course dogs in this case), but Cahill and Walker managed to hold things down even in the face of an adorable, overweight corgi. It’s a testament to the chemistry these two have on screen.

It has been revealed that their characters don’t share as much time on screen together as some of the other couples in Hallmark’s Christmas movies. However, the time they are together is swoonworthy — well, once they got over their meet-cute, that is. I definitely wouldn’t mind a sequel revisiting Goldie and Cohen a year from now. Or, better yet, I’d love to see Cahill and Walker star in even more Hallmark movies together now that it’s clear that they play compelling and entertaining romantic leads.

According to recent reports, blue Dog Valley might not be my favorite Hallmark Christmas movie of 2026, but it's still worth the watch. If you missed the live airing, you can stream it now with an active Hallmark+ subscription. While there, check out my favorite Cahill movie, Christmas on Cherry Lane, or my favorite Walker film, Three Wise Men and a Baby.

According to recent reports, A character named Mandy has the attention of many Grand Theft Auto 6 players--and that appears to include Reggie Fils-Aimé, the man who used to run Nintendo of America. Per GamesRadar, former Nintendo marketing and public relations manager Krysta Yang joked on social media that GTA 6, which is front-loaded with a lot of simulation-like busywork in the first chapter, is "adult Animal Crossing," posting images that highlight parallels between GTA 6 and Animal Crossing: New Horizons. Fils-Aimé quoted the post, saying: "If so, where's Mandy?" It's slightly eyebrow raising that the former executive for a family-friendly firm like Nintendo seems to have a strong opinion for a rather promiscuous video game character. No judgment to Fils-Aimé, of course, but talk around Mandy carries a certain... tone. Minor spoilers for the early parts of GTA 6 follow. https://twitter.com/Reggie/status/2123617589448384828?a=Qx10ccCT9noxvM3_aRc&s=20 One of the earliest missions in GTA 6 has Jason stopping by Mandy's home to collect rent. Long story short, she flirts pretty aggressively with Jason, who clearly isn't reciprocating, and Mandy doesn't take it well. And no, even if players wanted to, you can't romance Mandy. It doesn't help that it's implied that Mandy carries a dark secret, with Jason discovering a severed finger while fixing her sink's pipes. I'm not sure if anyone in Animal Crossing is that shady. So what does this post say about Reggie Fils-Aimé as a person? It's unclear what he thinks of the character--all we know is that he'd really like to know who the Animal Crossing equivalent of Mandy would be. It certainly wouldn't be Isabelle, so take your pick of any weird villagers you've encountered. Either way, it seems that Fils-Aimé is playing GTA 6 like the rest of us or, at the very least, is in tune with the massive cultural zeitgeist the game has produced.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when my partner and I were starting a family, we searched high and low for a place outside Upcoming York where we could imagine our future children growing up. We looked upstate, in Connecticut, and at all those charming hamlets strung along the eastern end of Long Island known as the Hamptons. Toured hundreds of houses, clicked thousands of listings. But not one felt like home.

Nevins in her garden in East Hampton.

It looked like something out of a medieval fairy tale. A great furrowed trunk rising from a froth of flowering vines that split into enormous limbs sweeping improbably far across the garden. Its arrangement was so baroque—veiny, muscular wood twisting and reaching, dissolving overhead into a canopy of green delicacy. We could picture our children climbing its winding branches, little hands against its ridged, mossy bark.

Sources indicate that our twins’ arrival was imminent, so we made an offer in February, closed in April, and brought home babies Grace and Noah on Memorial Day weekend. Now we joke that we didn’t buy a house—we bought this tree.

In a recent development, but what is it? A butternut tree? An oak? A black walnut? Deborah Nevins, one of the most revered living landscape designers, created this garden for the previous owners in 2004. In the fall, she invited me to her white-shingled cottage in Springs, East Hampton, to find out. Her living room has triple-hung windows like those in Monticello, Thomas Jefferson’s house in Virginia, which go down to the floor so it’s easy to wheel in her potted lemon trees when the seasons change. “Winter is divine; it’s when they bloom,” she coos. “The house smells of lemon blossoms.”.

David Geffen’s pool at his former Beverly Hills estate, once home to Warner Bros.’ Jack Warner.

It has been revealed that “Butternut!” she declares, slamming the book shut with all the force of her petite five-foot-nothing frame. “For sure.”.

This is our tree. A butternut that likely sprouted generations before she came along. “It’s a native tree, probably a hundred years old. But I’d have to know the caliper—the diameter about a foot up—to be more precise.” She decided it’d be the anchor for our yard design the moment she saw it—existing mature trees are “sacred” and must be preserved at all costs. At its base, she dared to plant clematis, usually a climbing vine, that now rambles across the ground, softening the old tree’s trunk with a tangle of flowers. The butternut divides the rest of the property into distinct passages, including an ornamental reflecting pool bordered by hornbeam hedges, a lap pool shaded under locust trees, and a gravel path lined with rounded boxwoods.

It has been revealed that GREEK MYTHOLOGY It took Nevins eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete her collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center. What was once a parking lot is now planted with more than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs.

A rendering of the 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens.

To Nevins, the tree is an excellent example of her greater gardening philosophy: “I’m interested in creating unfolding spaces which intensify [the viewers’] experience, your sense of place and movement through a garden,” she says. She frequently builds hedges and allées to control viewers’ attention, like horse blinders. “Not every aspect of the garden is seen at once. You have to stop and think.”.

According to recent reports, over the last four decades, Nevins has been entrusted with the grounds of some extraordinary spaces. Her clients include media mogul David Geffen, fashion designer Tommy Hilfiger, former Disney chairman Michael Eisner, and hotelier Ian Schrager. Commissions can range from tiny residential spaces (like mine) to huge commercial projects abroad. It took her eight years and some 20 trips to Greece to complete a 40-acre park at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Center in Athens. That was a collaboration with architect Renzo Piano on a landscape that climbs over the buildings themselves, planted with native grasses from the hills of Attica and fragrant Mediterranean herbs, including lavender, rosemary, and oregano. Nevins’s mantra for the project was simple: “Speak Greek.” The execution was anything but simple. More than 1,500 trees, 128,000 shrubs and perennials, and 164,000 grass plugs fill the public work. Nevins conceptualized the totality of the park. “I chose every single tree!” she claims. “We had to propagate hundreds of thousands of plants throughout Greece, and we decided to hire various nurseries so that if there was a disease or fire, the entire crop would not be wiped out.” Her effort impressed Piano. “It is always special when, beyond the work on a project itself, you realize that you share the same values and ideas,” says Piano of Nevins, whom he describes as a “wonderful professional and human adventure.”.

Industry observers note that “There is discipline in her work but never rigidity,” says Scott Mitchell, the West Coast–based architect who met Nevins at a dinner honoring architect Richard Meier in 1997 and went on to work with her on properties for Geffen in both California and New York. “Her landscapes don’t compete with architecture; they give it a place to belong.”.

He recalls the “emotional power” of her work for Geffen at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, former home of Warner Bros. cofounder Jack Warner. “Endless sweeps of white azaleas, a driveway lined with ancient, gnarled native sycamores, and 11 acres of rolling meadow beneath giant coast live oaks,” Mitchell states. “World-class projects require cohesion between architecture and landscape. They have to play from the same sheet of music. Debby totally gets that. Her response to architecture is clear and harmonious—confident but never overstepping.”.

Tommy Hilfiger and Dee Ocleppo at their Mustique estate.

Gil Schafer, a Fresh York–based architect who has worked with Nevins on more than 25 houses and gardens, also commends her command of structure. At his own house near Millbrook, she built a 12-foot-high hornbeam enclosure nestled into the surrounding farm fields that has, he notes, “an almost abstract sculptural quality—as if Richard Serra had suddenly decided to work in hornbeam rather than Corten steel.”.

It has been revealed that nevins was born in Manhattan at what was then the Doctors Hospital on the Upper East Side. The family resided in the penthouse of the same building where Greta Garbo lived. Her father died of a brain tumor at 43, when Nevins was six months old, and so her mother had to return to work. At six, she was sent to Camp Taconic in Massachusetts. “I was tiny! My mother might have been arrested today.” She remembers walking in the woods, finding a strawberry, and reporting the discovery in a letter home. The seed had been planted—pun quite obvious.

Industry observers note that fleur Cowles, the formidable editor behind the short-lived, extravagantly inventive magazine Flair, was a maternal relative and had an outsize impact on her childhood. “She knew everyone, and she was so brilliant,” Nevins indicates, offering me an problem of Flair from another bookshelf like a cherished family heirloom. Another influence was her mother’s sister, Miriam Sampson, an interior decorator who lived across from Carnegie Hall. “In this substantial apartment, she had her office in one room, and she had little models of apartments. I was so intrigued,” Nevins recalls. She’d cut out pictures of interiors and gardens from magazines and assemble them in scrapbooks. “But I didn’t even know about this idea of being a landscape architect.”.

Sources indicate that when Nevins was 14, her mother remarried and the family moved to Upcoming Haven, Connecticut. She went on to attend Boston University for undergrad and returned to New York for graduate school at Columbia. “They didn’t think that landscape history, which is what I wanted to study, was academic enough. And they probably had no one to teach it anyway,” she notes. So she earned an MA and an MPhil in art history. Travel became a form of individualized study. “I learned by looking,” she says. She sought out Le Corbusier’s buildings in France, including La Tourette, Maisons Jaoul, and Villa Savoye, and drove from Paris to Santiago de Compostela looking at Romanesque and Merovingian churches. She made her first of many pilgrimages to Sissinghurst, a garden in Kent created by the writer Vita Sackville-West and her diplomat husband, Harold Nicolson. “There’s nothing more beautiful than Sissinghurst,” she sighs.

One of Nevins’s greatest champions has been Geffen, whom Victoria Newhouse, the renowned architecture critic and widow of longtime Condé Nast chairman Si Newhouse, introduced her to. On her first meeting with Geffen, Nevins arrived to present her work with a carousel of 80 slides. “After maybe 30 slides, he states, ‘That’s enough. You’re hired.’ And I thought to myself, Who is this guy?” When she looked him up, she read that one of his attributes is spotting talent. “And that was that.”.

Industry observers note that at the Warner estate in Beverly Hills, she removed one swimming pool to open up the landscape, built a new one with a new patio house where Warner had a putting green, and relocated several mature oak trees on the property. “David is not afraid of big moves,” she notes. (They preserved the fountains and terraces Warner had commissioned from Florence Yoch, who designed the grounds of Tara for Gone With the Wind, of course.) However, according to Nevins, when Warner’s daughter came to see what Geffen had done, she looked around and asked if they had changed anything. “ ‘What did we change? We changed everything!’ ” Nevins remembers Geffen saying. “The idea that we didn’t do a thing is crazy, but that it looked like it was meant to be—that’s a good thing. The ultimate compliment that looks like I did nothing.”.

An aerial view of Deborah Nevins’s Hamptons garden.

Sources indicate that hilfiger hired Nevins for a property in Mustique in the early 1990s, and again for his Denbigh Farm in Greenwich in 1995. In the Caribbean, she created palm promenades and a courtyard of white flowers; in Connecticut, she brought the elements of an old estate into a coherent whole. “I knew she was incredibly passionate about her work, and that always interested me because I love working with people who are passionate about what they do,” Hilfiger notes. “Her execution was impeccable, and she delivered exactly what she promised.”.

Nevins’s office is based in New York City, and she keeps between 5 and 10 new projects going at all times. “Almost any job is interesting unless I hear in advance that the people aren’t nice,” she states. “Also, art collectors, in my experience, have been great patrons. If you’re an art collector—and you’re truly not collecting just to make money from art—you have an interest in beauty and understanding.”.

PLEACHY KEEN “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say,” architect Gil Schafer says of Nevins. “She feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

Recent findings suggest that on average, it takes two years to get a garden up and running, three years if she needs to build fresh structures. But a garden is never finished. Roberta Denning, who with her husband, Steve, commissioned Nevins for her family’s property in Greenwich in 2006, describes the pleasure of living with something that acquires depth while continuing to change. “What she created has grown more valuable with time,” Denning notes of her property, which includes a walking labyrinth among chestnuts and beech trees. “Nearly 20 years on, the gardens feel both that they have always been here and that they are continually renewed.” Nevins says clients have joked that hiring her is like a marriage because it’s a long-term relationship, and it requires work. “So I guess I’m a polygamist?” she smiles.

According to recent reports, patience is a massive part of her process. “She is very intuitive, so she needs to walk a site and feel what it has to say, and this is one way that we are so similar in our approach,” Schafer says. “You need to give her the space to read the land and sort out how she wants to approach it. I think she also feels this deep kinship with the natural world, with plants and with the trees of a site, which guides how she approaches her interventions on a property.”.

In a recent development, people joke that Nevins speaks to the plants, but Schafer isn’t sure it’s an act. “I think she really does!”.

In a recent development, “I do love them,” Nevins indicates of her botanical family. “I was at a nursery with someone the other day, and I said, ‘It’s problematic. I get crushes on plants, but sometimes they don’t really have a place, and it’s so disappointing. It’s like a failed romance.’”.

A walking labyrinth in Greenwich, Connecticut.

According to recent reports, presently her crush is Stewartia pseudocamellia. “It has amazing bark, and the flower looks like a camellia, but it’s not a camellia, it’s a tree.” One plant she doesn’t love? Flowering forsythia, which Schafer reports she often refers to as “spring vomit.”.

Nevins believes her greatest asset is the ability to blend both architectural history and botanical skill. “I have such a strong academic background in architectural history,” she says. “I know exactly what these references are that they make to historical, even modern historical buildings.”.

In another part of Long Island, Nevins combined the elements into what she calls a “beech house”—pun absolutely intentional. Martin Filler, an architecture critic and longtime contributor to The Fresh York Review of Books, met Nevins when they were graduate students in Columbia’s art history department in the early 1970s. At the time, his wife, Rosemarie Haag Bletter, an architectural historian and professor emerita of art history at the CUNY Graduate Center in New York City, was working on her PhD and teaching undergraduates. According to Filler, Nevins promised back then to design them a garden one day. “Since we didn’t have a house and never expected to, we mentioned to ourselves, ‘Yeah, right,’ ” he indicates. “But who knew that someday we would, and that gardening would become such a large part of our lives, especially Rosemarie’s?”.

Recent findings suggest that in the mid-1990s, they bought a cottage that had been part of Stanford White’s Breese estate, The Orchard, in Southampton. “Debby remarked that she would now make good on her promise to design a garden for us,” Filler remembers. “By that time she had become one of the top landscape designers, but she insisted on doing it and refused to be paid.” She stayed with them for a winter weekend and spent hours walking the property. “Then she sat down at our dining table with a roll of yellow tracing paper and the surveyor’s map, and she designed the whole thing within a few hours. She joked, ‘Don’t tell anyone how fast I was.’ ”.

In a recent development, THE GIVING TREE When Derek C. Blasberg first saw the majestic tree in the backyard of a property in the Hamptons, he knew he’d found a home for his family. The hunt to identify it led him to Nevins’s larger body of work. “We could picture our children climbing its winding branches.”.

The Beech House, a 16-foot-by-16-foot-by-16-foot living gazebo made of 26 purple beech trees (Fagus sylvatica “Dawyck Purple”), is the centerpiece. The trees were sourced from Buffalo, trucked to Southampton, and replanted in the same orientation in which they had been grown. (“Each tree had to be marked with a dot of blue paint to indicate due north and then planted in that same geographical direction,” Filler remembers.) They were wired and trained over a wooden inner framework shaped like the schematic outline of a house and then clipped into shape on the exterior. The floor was paved with bluestone squares and rectangles in a random-looking pattern Nevins designed.

“Each year when we meet with our accountant to do our tax return, he’s always shocked that we spend so much on the garden,” Filler indicates. “We tell him: ‘You have clients who have boats, you have clients who have classic cars—well, this is our pleasure, our indulgence.’”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fresh off the finish line of the 2026 NYC Marathon, Antoni Porowski has a major milestone to celebrate this holiday season — but he admits he couldn’t have done it without the support of a special someone cheering him on every step of the way.

The Queer Eye star, 42, exclusively opened up to Us about how his partner, Zacharias Niedzwiecki, a personal trainer and Peloton yoga and strength instructor, helped him prepare for the grueling 26.2-mile race.

According to recent reports, “I have to give him credit where credit’s due,” Porowski told Us. “The only reason I was able to get through that is he understands my body. He made sure that I was doing plenty of yoga and stretches and preparing, because I don’t know how any of this stuff works, and he literally does that for a living, so I was super lucky to have someone literally by my side the entire time.”.

After spending just three months preparing for the urban trek across Upcoming York City’s five boroughs, Porowski described the experience as one of the hardest of his life.

“It was the best of times and it was the worst of times when you’re running through the streets and you have complete strangers cheering because, like, your name is on your banner,” he recalled. “There’s something really beautiful and sort of like very community-driven about the whole city, New York.”.

One of the most difficult moments, he indicates, came during the notorious silence that sweeps the Queensboro Bridge, where the cheers of spectators faded, leaving only the sound of runners’ sneakers hitting the pavement and the drive to push through. But by the final eight miles, he says it didn’t take long for him to understand why so many runners return for another marathon.

It has been revealed that “That’s how I felt the first five minutes when my partner asked me how I felt,” he joked when asked whether he ever wanted to run again. “But later that night, I was on social media and I was scrolling and I was listening to the cowbells and there was something very soothing in that.”.

With 2027 just around the corner, Porowski shared he is already entertaining the idea of taking his next marathon overseas, potentially combining his love for running with his passion for travel. “Maybe it’s Paris or Berlin or London or some kind of a marathon next year,” he told Us. “I’m not ready to think about it yet, but I’m also excited, and I’m thinking like, what else can I do?”.

But before committing to another finish line, Porowski is shifting his focus to the holidays — partnering with Marshalls for its Unwrap the Internet campaign, which rolled out November 10 alongside Lindsay Lohan, Danny Pellegrino and Robin Arzón.

It has been revealed that as part of the initiative, the food and travel enthusiast curated the “Frequent Flyers” holiday gift guide, featuring everything from silk sleep masks and toiletry kits to travel-sized skin essentials. The partnership also brings back fond memories for Porowski, who grew up visiting Marshalls with his family and remembers the excitement he felt exploring everything the retailer had to offer.

Recent findings suggest that “Well, to quote my therapist, if it’s hysterical, it’s historical, and one of my favorite experiences shopping with my family was always going to Marshalls,” Porowski told Us. “I know that I might be the travel expert, but going through the entire food section, like all of the kitchen appliances and then clothing, it truly always felt like the one place that we could go to where everyone was happy because there truly is something for everybody.”.

When it comes to holiday gifting, Porowski said he refuses to “gatekeep secrets”, though he admits Niedzwiecki, 33, has reminded him that the perfect present isn’t always something he’d pick out for himself.

It has been revealed that “If I experience something amazing, I need you to try it because I want you to experience the same joy of either the novelty popcorn or the dopp kit or whatever it is,” he told Us. “But sometimes I get into trouble because my partner also reminds me to try to put myself in the other person’s shoes, and try to imagine what they actually need.”.

Porowski says that when it comes to gift-giving, he has also learned to weigh how practical a present is for the recipient’s lifestyle, joking that candles might not be the best choice for households with curious cats—something he knows firsthand now that he is a father to two felines at home.

With NYC Marathon training behind him and the holiday shopping sprint underway, Porowski already has his sights set on another kind of marathon—binge-watching The Real Housewives of Fresh York City.

Although he admits he hasn’t tuned in to season 16 yet, the longtime Bravo fan says he is especially eager to watch his friend Daisy Toye stir things up on the show.

According to recent reports, “I actually know Daisy really well from our lives outside of TV, and I heard that she is really bringing in a lot of entertainment this season,” he told Us. “I can’t wait because I know how her brain operates, and she says exactly what she thinks.”.

Carole Radziwill also makes the list of Housewives he can’t wait to watch, making no secret of his excitement surrounding her return to the franchise. “The voice of reason, who is all of us, Carole Radziwill is back, which I think is so beautiful, and I loved her book. I love everything about her. I just think she’s an absolute icon, and so I’m excited to revisit.”.

But before he can settle in for a much-anticipated RHONY binge, he has one more challenge ahead of him — getting Niedzwiecki to join in on the Bravo drama.

“I just have to convince my partner because he’s typically into, like, David Attenborough natural history docs, and this is a different type of social study, Housewives,” Porowski told Us. “So as long as I convince him to watch it with me.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • East Asia--and particularly Japan--has been suffering a rash of cybersecurity incidents as of late, affecting everything from major banks and cellphone service providers to city governments and small businesses.
  • East Asia--and particularly Japan--has been suffering a rash of cybersecurity incidents as of late, affecting everything from major banks and cellphone service providers to city governments and small businesses.
  • Industry observers note that one recent incident involved the PC launcher for the popular gacha action shooter NIKKE: Goddess of Victory, where malicious code would install a trojan called k2f that would compromise an individual's PC, taking screenshots, logging inputs, and installing/executing programs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

East Asia--and particularly Japan--has been suffering a rash of cybersecurity incidents as of late, affecting everything from major banks and cellphone service providers to city governments and small businesses. Gaming has been one of many areas targeted: between arcade games on Sega's network going offline, 11 million Capcom IDs being compromised, and a high-schooler hacking Bandai-Namco, some major publishers have been suffering a string of embarrassments. One recent incident involved the PC launcher for the popular gacha action shooter NIKKE: Goddess of Victory, where malicious code would install a trojan called k2f that would compromise an individual's PC, taking screenshots, logging inputs, and installing/executing programs. Unfortunately for one Japanese municipality, someone's gacha habits may have lead to a much bigger incident. Iwamizawa is a city of about 75,000 located in Hokkaido, Japan's northernmost island. It's not a place that makes a lot of news, but it recently went viral on the Japanese-speaking side of social media. As reported by Automaton, the city issued a notice that an IT sub-sub-contractor handling the city's fixed asset records suffered a security breach--specifically, a k2f hijack. Observers soon surmised that the most likely source of k2f would be someone playing a certain sexy gacha game on a work PC. The subcontractor in question, IT services company GIS Hokkaido, would then confirm to Japanese tech news site ITMedia that, yes, NIKKE's compromised PC launcher was the source of the problem. When asked if an employee or subcontractor had launched the game on a work PC, GIS politely replied that "they would prefer not to comment." Moral of the story? While there's nothing wrong with playing a suggestive gacha game on your own time, you probably shouldn't do it on the clock, and definitely not on a company PC, lest you become internet meme fodder.
